title.narrative: Multi-sector emergency assistance for vulnerable population

description.narrative: IDPs, returnees and most vulnerable host communities are project target groups of the project. Furthermore, The Project will involve the (a) vulnerable women & girls - including female headed household, (b) People with special needs (PSN)/People with disabilities (PWD), (c) elderly headed household, (d) child headed household, and (e) vulnerable household with children under 5 years old and/or pregnant/lactating women as the marginalised groups to be included from the beginning of the Project process (i.e. socialisation about the project, beneficiary selection, and assessment) up to Project's monitoring. Their involvement will be considered as the inclusion for protection that is considered as the cross-cutting theme in Project’s actions.

The Taliban's takeover in 2021 brought significant changes to Afghanistan, resulting in a massive outflux of people and a sharp decline in development and investment that had been ongoing since 2002. This situation, exacerbated by natural disasters and ongoing armed conflicts in some areas, has pushed many Afghans to the brink of poverty. The economic crisis, characterized by high unemployment, a scarce job market, and soaring inflation, has severely impacted the country's resilience. Consequently, when disasters strike, local populations often struggle to respond in a timely manner due to their diminished capacity and resilience, leading to an inability to cope and a slow recovery process for communities and public infrastructure. Afghanistan continues to face entrenched poverty, climate-induced crises, and barriers to women’s equality and participation in public life. Afghanistan remains primarily a protection emergency characterized by high levels of protracted displacement, forced repatriation, mine and explosive ordnance contamination, restrictions to freedom of movement, increased risk of gender-based violence, child labour, early marriage and increased needs for mental health and psychosocial support. It is estimated that in the current year 2024, around 23.7 million people representing more than half of the population of Afghanistan would require humanitarian assistance. According to the recent IPC acute food insecurity analysis report, during October 2023 – March 2024 (the winter lean season), nearly 15.8 million people in Afghanistan experienced high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above), almost increase 7% from the same season last year (13.1 million). Out of 15.8 million people, 12.2 million will likely be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and 3.6 million in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). The IPC report shows hat emergencies are expected to significantly increase in the projection analysis period from 38 to 45 analytical domains. Afghanistan also faces a climate-induced emergency, with the country in the midst of its third consecutive year of drought-like conditions, following the worst drought in 30 years in 2021/2022. Rising temperatures are rapidly altering precipitation patterns across the country, diminishing people’s access to water. Increases in drought related shocks were reported in 15 out of 34 provinces. Anticipated El Niño conditions in late 2023 and early 2024, pose risk of flooding and crop pests. Water and sanitation conditions are sub-optimal, with little prospect of immediate improvement. Women in the most recent survey conducted by the UN outlined compounding challenges in their living conditions, including potential harassment of DFA officials and community members, a lack of education, basic services and transportation, unemployment, mobility restrictions, and economic difficulties. Targeting Nangarhar, Urozgan, and Herat, the Project aims to support disaster-affected populations, including the large influx of forced returnees from Pakistan and Iran, and particularly the vulnerable communities in Herat following the October 2023 earthquake. The selected districts in these provinces are remote and prone to natural disasters such as floods and prolonged droughts. Needs assessments have identified multiple critical issues, with confirmed high levels of food insecurity. Local communities have expressed significant concerns about food security, lack of income, limited livelihood opportunities, and womenfocused health and safety support.

Vulnerable People (including women, men, girls and boys) have ensured survival through accessible, timely, effective, and inclusive food security, winterization and women-focused health and safety support interventions in Herat, Daikundi, and Nangarhar Provinces of Afghanistan.
